t: How A Party Can Improve Classroom Management gement/
q: It’s a clean-the-room party . And the way it works is simple: one day a week you will supervise a thorough cleaning of your classroom.
Whenever you introduce something new, it’s important to model what you want . To that end, show your students exactly how to perform each job successfully.
Put music on. Let your students work in teams. Let them talk and laugh and have a good time together .
It’s also a good time to pair up with your most difficult student. Working together is a great way to build trust and rapport.
There is something about doing physical work that clicks with students. A weekly cleaning party can impart the virtues of cooperation and hard work better than anything we can say to them.

t: The 7 Rules Of Handling Difficult Students
q: Unfortunately, the frustrations you feel dealing with difficult students can cause you to make mistakes.
It’s normal for teachers to force explanations from difficult students as a form of accountability. But asking why and demanding a response from them almost always ends in resentment.

Teachers often shower difficult students with praise for doing what is minimally expected. But because these students can look around at their fellow classmates and know that it’s a sham, false praise doesn’t work.
Every day is a new day” should be your mantra with difficult students. They need to know that they have a clean slate to start each day–and so do you.

Your classroom management plan merely nudges them in the right direction. Done correctly, it gets students to look inward, to self-evaluate, and to feel the weight of their transgressions. But by itself, it can only do so much.

t: How To Improve Classroom Management By Talking Less https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2011/04/16/improve-classroom-management-by-talking-less/
q: Many teachers make the mistake of trying to talk their students through each moment of the school day.
But it doesn’t work. Too much talking has the opposite effect. It makes classroom management more difficult.
When you let your classroom management plan do your talking for you, you can eliminate lecturing, pleading, yelling, scolding, arguing, and the like from your school day.
Many teachers repeat everything they say–sometimes three and four times. When you repeat yourself, you weaken your words and encourage students to ignore you.
The more efficient and direct you can be with your words, the more effective your teaching will be.
By limiting the amount of talking you do, you’ll have more time to get to know your students.
My challenge is to use the suggestions above to try cutting your talking by a third. If you do, you’ll find yourself speaking with more power and impact.

t: How To Improve Attentiveness In 5 Minutes
q: Your students are chatty and distracted. Their heads are on a swivel. They’re squirming in their seats. Only the most dedicated appear to be following along.
The problem with these methods is that they’re unlikely to work for more than a few minutes. The fact is, regardless of how old they are, your students can only sit and attend for so long.
An exercise break is an easy and effective strategy that also happens to be backed by science.
After just five minutes of moderate exercise, your students will be refreshed, recharged, and ready to learn.
When combined with exercise, music clears the mind and improves mental performance.
I’ve found that if you schedule your exercise breaks–once in the morning and once in the afternoon–your students will look forward to them.

t: Do Your Students Know You're In Charge?
q: There is a lot that stands out in your mind while teaching students from both ends of the classroom management spectrum. But one thing is indisputable. In classrooms with poor classroom management, the students believe they are, to some degree, in charge.
When a teacher leaves a leadership vacuum of any kind, and to any degree, the students will fill it with a vengeance.

Your students may not yet be able to write a coherent paragraph, read at grade level, or tie their shoes, but if they’re unsure about who the ultimate authority in the classroom is, they’ll tell you how you should do your job.
Absent of strong leadership, there is no sense of urgency in students, no bright-eyed enthusiasm, and little work ethic.
The fact is, when a teacher reveals him or herself as less than the ultimate authority in the classroom, the students will exploit it for all it’s worth.
I’m your teacher and I’m in charge of this classroom. That’s my job. That means I make the decisions. I decide how you behave, what we learn, how we learn, and when we do the things we do.
Deep down our students don’t want to slouch or goof off or tell us how to do our jobs. They do it because they’re uninspired.
